newsitem.title: USA: J&L says steel imports beginning to ease.
newsitem.headline: J&L says steel imports beginning to ease.

text.p: Specialty steel imports that have been flooding the domestic market for months are beginning to ease, giving U.S. producers a shot at recouping some of the profitability they have lost over the past year, the chief executive of J&L Specialty Steel Inc said Tuesday.

"Currently, imports are below 1996 levels," Claude Kronk said at the company's annual meeting. "No one knows if this trend will continue, but it's indicative of improving market conditions in Europe."

Sluggish foreign economies sent a heavy level of specialty steel imports to the more lucrative U.S. market in 1996. As a result, U.S. producers saw their earnings fall as imports put downward pressure on selling prices.
J&L posted net income last year of $24.3 million, or $0.63 per share, versus $84.4 million, or $2.18 per share, in 1995.
Kronk said things have been improving so far this year due to lower imports and two 5 percent price increases implemented by U.S. producers. But he said '97 "will be a challenge."
"The first half of '97 isn't going to look so good," he said. "(If we're going to improve our earnings performance from '96) we're going to have to do it in the second half of the year."
Wall Street's consensus estimate for the year is $0.11 per share, based on seven estimates with a wide range, from a loss of $0.25 to a gain of $0.50.

Kronk noted that despite the difficulty in industry pricing, the company's order rate from customers is strong and U.S. specialty steel consumption will increase by more than 4 percent this year over last year.
"In other words, we've had profitless prosperity," he said. "Pricing and imports will play a key role (in our performance this year.")
Separately, Kronk, 65, said he will retire as chief executive officer at the end of the year. He was named chief executive in 1986.
